props.title: The Secret Six

sections.content: The Secret Six (1931) stands as a pivotal pre-Code gangster film, arriving in the same explosive year as Little Caesar (1931) and The Public Enemy (1931). MGM's entry into the gangster genre features a young Clark Gable in a supporting role, marking one of his earliest significant appearances before becoming Hollywood's "King." The film's raw portrayal of corruption, violence, and organized crime pushed boundaries during the pre-Code era, when filmmakers could explore darker themes before the Production Code's strict enforcement in 1934.

sections.content: Director George Hill crafted The Secret Six as a ripped-from-the-headlines exposé, basing it on Chicago's real-life "Secret Six" Committee of businessmen who fought organized crime. The film stars Wallace Beery as "Slaughterhouse" Scorpio, a butcher who rises in the criminal underworld, with Jean Harlow as the moll caught between rival gangsters. Its blend of newspaper reporting and criminal investigation influenced later crime films like Call Northside 777 (1948) and The Street with No Name (1948).

The film's lasting impact can be seen in how it helped establish crucial gangster film conventions - the rise-and-fall narrative, corrupt political connections, and journalists as crusading heroes. These elements would become standard in films like The Roaring Twenties (1939) and Force of Evil (1948), showing how early gangster pictures shaped the crime genre for decades to come. sections.content: The Secret Six exemplifies how pre-Code Hollywood tackled social issues head-on. Like contemporary films Night World (1932) and Beast of the City (1932), it portrayed violence and corruption with unprecedented frankness. The film's depiction of political corruption and organized crime's infiltration of legitimate business presaged later exposés like On the Waterfront (1954) and The Phenix City Story (1955).
